cards.q: What is AWS IAM?
cards.a: Global service: users, groups, roles and policies for access to AWS

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Global service: users, groups, roles and policies for access to AWS”
cards.a: AWS IAM

cards.q: When would you choose AWS IAM?
cards.a:
• Need to give an app on EC2/Lambda access to S3/DynamoDB → IAM role
• Least privilege, MFA, temporary credentials
• Cross-account access → role + trust policy (AssumeRole)
• Machines → IAM role (instance profile); humans (admins) → MFA + least privilege

cards.q: AWS IAM: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Global (not regional); everything is denied by default (implicit deny)
• Explicit Deny always wins over Allow
• Identity-based vs resource-based policies (S3 bucket policy, KMS key policy)
• Roles for EC2/Lambda (instance profile) instead of access keys on the instance
• Permissions boundary caps the maximum permissions of a user/role
• Root: enable MFA, don't use it for everyday tasks

cards.q: When is AWS IAM NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Storing access keys in code/AMI is a trap — use a role
• Authenticating users of a mobile/web app — that's Cognito
• An IAM user per EC2 instance — that's just long-term keys again; use a role

cards.q: AWS IAM vs AWS STS: what's the difference?
cards.a: STS issues temporary credentials on AssumeRole; IAM defines roles and permissions

cards.q: AWS IAM vs AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO): what's the difference?
cards.a: Identity Center — SSO for people across many accounts; IAM — within a single account

cards.q: AWS IAM vs Service Control Policies (SCP): what's the difference?
cards.a: An SCP caps the maximum for an account; it grants nothing by itself

cards.q: What is AWS STS?
cards.a: Issues temporary security credentials (AssumeRole, federation)

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Issues temporary security credentials (AssumeRole, federation)”
cards.a: AWS STS

cards.q: When would you choose AWS STS?
cards.a:
• Temporary access to another account
• Federation with a corporate IdP (SAML)
• Requirement to not store long-lived keys

cards.q: AWS STS: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• AssumeRole, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, AssumeRoleWithSAML, GetSessionToken (MFA)
• Credentials last from 15 min to 12 h (1 h by default)
• Cross-account: role trust policy + sts:AssumeRole permission for the caller
• Regional endpoints available (better latency/redundancy)

cards.q: When is AWS STS NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Not a user directory and not an SSO portal

cards.q: AWS STS vs AWS IAM: what's the difference?
cards.a: IAM defines roles/policies; STS issues temporary keys based on them

cards.q: AWS STS vs Amazon Cognito: what's the difference?
cards.a: Cognito Identity Pools obtain STS credentials for app users under the hood

cards.q: What is AWS Organizations?
cards.a: Centralized management of many accounts: OUs, SCPs, consolidated billing

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Centralized management of many accounts: OUs, SCPs, consolidated billing”
cards.a: AWS Organizations

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Organizations?
cards.a:
• Many accounts, need a single bill and discounts
• Deny actions/Regions across a group of accounts at once
• Create accounts automatically via API

cards.q: AWS Organizations: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Management account + member accounts, grouped into OUs
• Modes: consolidated billing only or all features — SCPs and IAM Identity Center require all features
• Consolidated billing: one bill, volume discounts, shared RI/Savings Plans pool
• SCPs apply to OUs/accounts (not to the management account)
• Tag policies, backup policies, AI opt-out policies
• Organization CloudTrail trail for all accounts

cards.q: When is AWS Organizations NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• On its own it doesn't give a landing zone with guardrails — that's Control Tower
• No "external authentication" — directory sign-in is done by IAM Identity Center
• Has no authentication of its own to point at Directory Service — sign-in via IAM Identity Center

cards.q: AWS Organizations vs AWS Control Tower: what's the difference?
cards.a: Control Tower automates a multi-account landing zone on top of Organizations

cards.q: AWS Organizations vs Service Control Policies (SCP): what's the difference?
cards.a: SCP is an Organizations feature for restricting permissions

cards.q: What is Service Control Policies (SCP)?
cards.a: Guardrails in Organizations: maximum permissions for accounts/OUs

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Guardrails in Organizations: maximum permissions for accounts/OUs”
cards.a: Service Control Policies (SCP)

cards.q: When would you choose Service Control Policies (SCP)?
cards.a:
• Prevent all accounts in an OU from using certain services/Regions
• Even the root of a member account must not be able to do X
• Centralized preventive control

cards.q: Service Control Policies (SCP): what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• They grant no permissions — they only restrict (a filter)
• Apply to all users/roles in the account, including root
• Don't apply to the management account or service-linked roles
• Effective permissions = intersection of SCPs and IAM policies
• Typical: deny outside allowed Regions, deny disabling CloudTrail

cards.q: When is Service Control Policies (SCP) NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Doesn't grant access — an Allow in an SCP without an IAM policy gives nothing
• Doesn't affect the management account

cards.q: Service Control Policies (SCP) vs AWS IAM: what's the difference?
cards.a: IAM policy grants permissions; SCP sets the upper bound

cards.q: Service Control Policies (SCP) vs AWS Config: what's the difference?
cards.a: Config — detective (detect), SCP — preventive (deny)

cards.q: What is AWS Control Tower?
cards.a: Fast multi-account landing zone with ready-made guardrails

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Fast multi-account landing zone with ready-made guardrails”
cards.a: AWS Control Tower

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Control Tower?
cards.a:
• Set up a multi-account environment per best practices with LEAST operational overhead
• Automatic setup of new accounts with guardrails
• "Streamline creating many accounts with preapproved baselines/network configs per OU" → Control Tower (Account Factory)

cards.q: AWS Control Tower: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Built on Organizations, Identity Center, CloudTrail, Config
• Controls (guardrails): preventive (SCP), detective (Config), proactive (CloudFormation hooks)
• Account Factory — provisions new accounts per OU from preapproved baselines (incl. VPC/network config); built on Service Catalog
• Per-account compliance dashboard

cards.q: When is AWS Control Tower NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Overkill for a single account

cards.q: AWS Control Tower vs AWS Organizations: what's the difference?
cards.a: Organizations is the base mechanism; Control Tower is ready-made automation on top

cards.q: AWS Control Tower vs AWS Config: what's the difference?
cards.a: Config — rule evaluation/visibility; Control Tower — account vending + guardrails (uses Config for detective controls)

cards.q: What is AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO)?
cards.a: SSO for employees into all Organizations accounts and business apps

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“SSO for employees into all Organizations accounts and business apps”
cards.a: AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO)

cards.q: When would you choose AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO)?
cards.a:
• Employees must sign in once to all AWS accounts
• Use corporate AD/Okta for access to AWS

cards.q: AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO): what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Formerly AWS SSO
• Identity source: built-in directory, Active Directory, external IdP (Okta, Entra ID) via SAML/SCIM
• Permission sets → IAM roles in target accounts
• Single sign-in portal
• Requires Organizations (all features); an existing on-prem AD connects via AD Connector or AWS Managed Microsoft AD (trust)

cards.q: When is AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Not for end users of your application — that's Cognito

cards.q: AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) vs Amazon Cognito: what's the difference?
cards.a: Cognito — application customers (B2C); Identity Center — employees (workforce)

cards.q: AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) vs AWS Directory Service: what's the difference?
cards.a: Directory Service can be an identity source for Identity Center

cards.q: AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) vs AWS IAM: what's the difference?
cards.a: IAM users — within one account; Identity Center — centrally across many

cards.q: What is Amazon Cognito?
cards.a: Authentication and authorization for web/mobile app users

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Authentication and authorization for web/mobile app users”
cards.a: Amazon Cognito

cards.q: When would you choose Amazon Cognito?
cards.a:
• Sign-up/sign-in for millions of mobile app users
• Mobile client needs direct access to S3/DynamoDB
• Login via Google/Facebook/Apple

cards.q: Amazon Cognito: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• User Pools: sign-up/sign-in, JWT tokens, MFA, social/SAML/OIDC login
• Identity Pools: exchange a token for temporary AWS credentials (STS)
• User Pool as an authorizer in API Gateway and ALB
• Guest (unauthenticated) access supported in Identity Pools

cards.q: When is Amazon Cognito NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Not for employee SSO into AWS accounts (that's Identity Center)

cards.q: Amazon Cognito vs AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO): what's the difference?
cards.a: Identity Center — employees; Cognito — app users

cards.q: Amazon Cognito vs AWS IAM: what's the difference?
cards.a: Don't create an IAM user per app user — use Cognito

cards.q: What is AWS Directory Service?
cards.a: Managed Microsoft AD and integration with on-prem Active Directory

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Managed Microsoft AD and integration with on-prem Active Directory”
cards.a: AWS Directory Service

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Directory Service?
cards.a:
• Apps in AWS need Active Directory / Kerberos / LDAP
• Use an existing on-prem AD without replication → AD Connector
• Trust between AWS and on-prem AD → Managed Microsoft AD
• Sign in to AWS accounts with existing on-prem AD credentials without copying them → AD Connector + IAM Identity Center

cards.q: AWS Directory Service: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• AWS Managed Microsoft AD — full AD, trust with on-prem AD
• AD Connector — proxy to on-prem AD, stores nothing in AWS
• Simple AD — cheap Samba-compatible, no trust
• Needed for FSx for Windows, WorkSpaces, RDS for SQL Server (Windows auth)

cards.q: When is AWS Directory Service NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • For authenticating mobile app users — Cognito

cards.q: AWS Directory Service vs AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO): what's the difference?
cards.a: Identity Center can use AD as an identity source

cards.q: What is AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM)?
cards.a: Share resources between accounts without copying

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Share resources between accounts without copying”
cards.a: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM)

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM)?
cards.a:
• Several accounts must use one VPC/subnets
• Share a Transit Gateway with all accounts in the organization

cards.q: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM): what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Shares: VPC subnets, Transit Gateway, Route 53 Resolver rules, License Manager, Aurora clusters, etc.
• Within Organizations or with individual accounts
• Shared VPC: participants launch resources in the owner's subnets
• No additional charge

cards.q: When is AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Doesn't grant IAM permissions to service APIs in general
• Cannot create accounts or enforce baselines — it only shares existing resources

cards.q: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) vs VPC Peering: what's the difference?
cards.a: Shared subnets via RAM — one VPC instead of peering many VPCs

cards.q: What is AWS KMS?
cards.a: Managed encryption keys, integrated with almost all services

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Managed encryption keys, integrated with almost all services”
cards.a: AWS KMS

cards.q: When would you choose AWS KMS?
cards.a:
• Encryption at rest with key management and auditing
• Need control over key rotation/policy → customer managed key
• Encrypted snapshot to another account/Region

cards.q: AWS KMS: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• AWS owned / AWS managed (aws/s3) / customer managed keys (CMK)
• Symmetric (AES-256) and asymmetric; direct encryption up to 4 KB, larger — envelope encryption (data key)
• Key policy is mandatory; access = key policy + IAM
• Automatic CMK rotation (yearly by default, configurable)
• Keys are regional; multi-Region keys for copying encrypted data
• All calls logged in CloudTrail; API quotas (throttling)

cards.q:
AWS KMS — fill in the blank:
Symmetric (AES-256) and asymmetric; direct encryption up to _____, larger — envelope encryption (data key)
cards.a:
4 KB

Symmetric (AES-256) and asymmetric; direct encryption up to 4 KB, larger — envelope encryption (data key)

cards.q: When is AWS KMS NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• FIPS 140-2 Level 3 / single-tenant HSM with full control requirement → CloudHSM
• Doesn't store passwords/secrets — that's Secrets Manager

cards.q: AWS KMS vs AWS CloudHSM: what's the difference?
cards.a: CloudHSM — dedicated HSM, only you manage the keys; KMS — managed multi-tenant

cards.q: AWS KMS vs AWS Secrets Manager: what's the difference?
cards.a: Secrets Manager stores secrets (and encrypts them via KMS)

cards.q: AWS KMS vs AWS Certificate Manager (ACM): what's the difference?
cards.a: ACM — TLS certificates, not data encryption keys

cards.q: What is AWS CloudHSM?
cards.a: Dedicated hardware HSM in a VPC, keys controlled only by the customer

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Dedicated hardware HSM in a VPC, keys controlled only by the customer”
cards.a: AWS CloudHSM

cards.q: When would you choose AWS CloudHSM?
cards.a:
• Regulatory requirement: dedicated HSM / Level 3 / full key control
• Oracle TDE, SSL offload, custom crypto operations

cards.q: AWS CloudHSM: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated, single-tenant
• AWS has no access to the keys; lose the credentials — lose the keys
• HSM cluster across multiple AZs for HA
• Can be attached as a custom key store for KMS
• Standard APIs: PKCS#11, JCE, CNG; SSL/TLS offload

cards.q: When is AWS CloudHSM NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • When managed encryption with LEAST operational overhead is enough → KMS

cards.q: AWS CloudHSM vs AWS KMS: what's the difference?
cards.a: KMS is simpler and integrated; CloudHSM — single-tenant with full customer control

cards.q: What is AWS Secrets Manager?
cards.a: Storage and automatic rotation of secrets (DB passwords, API keys)

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Storage and automatic rotation of secrets (DB passwords, API keys)”
cards.a: AWS Secrets Manager

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Secrets Manager?
cards.a:
• Store a DB password and rotate it automatically
• Remove credentials from application code

cards.q: AWS Secrets Manager: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Automatic rotation via Lambda; built-in for RDS/Aurora/Redshift/DocumentDB
• Encryption via KMS
• Replication of secrets to other Regions
• Paid per secret and per API call; up to 64 KB per secret

cards.q:
AWS Secrets Manager — fill in the blank:
Paid per secret and per API call; up to _____ per secret
cards.a:
64 KB

Paid per secret and per API call; up to 64 KB per secret

cards.q: When is AWS Secrets Manager NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • If rotation isn't needed and cost matters — SSM Parameter Store (SecureString)

cards.q: AWS Secrets Manager vs AWS Systems Manager: what's the difference?
cards.a: Parameter Store is cheaper/free, but has no built-in rotation

cards.q: AWS Secrets Manager vs AWS KMS: what's the difference?
cards.a: KMS manages keys; Secrets Manager manages the secrets themselves

cards.q: What is AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)?
cards.a: Free public TLS certificates with auto-renewal

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Free public TLS certificates with auto-renewal”
cards.a: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)?
cards.a:
• HTTPS on ALB/CloudFront with minimal maintenance
• Automatic certificate renewal

cards.q: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM): what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Integrations: ELB, CloudFront, API Gateway (not directly on EC2)
• For CloudFront the certificate must be in us-east-1
• Auto-renewal for ACM-issued certificates (DNS validation)
• Imported certificates are not renewed automatically
• Private CA — for internal certificates (paid)

cards.q: When is AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• A public ACM certificate cannot be exported to EC2/on-prem
• Not a store for AWS access keys or secrets — it manages TLS certificates (secrets → Secrets Manager)

cards.q: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) vs AWS KMS: what's the difference?
cards.a: KMS — data encryption keys; ACM — certificates for TLS in transit

cards.q: What is AWS WAF?
cards.a: Web Application Firewall at L7 (HTTP)

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Web Application Firewall at L7 (HTTP)”
cards.a: AWS WAF

cards.q: When would you choose AWS WAF?
cards.a:
• Protection against SQL injection / XSS
• Block IPs/countries on ALB or CloudFront
• Rate-limit requests from a single IP

cards.q: AWS WAF: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Attaches to ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito User Pool
• Web ACL: rules by IP, geo, headers, SQLi, XSS
• Rate-based rules against HTTP floods
• Managed rule groups (AWS and Marketplace)
• Doesn't work on NLB (L4)

cards.q: When is AWS WAF NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Doesn't protect NLB and doesn't filter L3/L4 traffic
• For L3/L4 DDoS → Shield
• Not a scaling/performance tool; attaches in front of ALB/CloudFront/API Gateway/AppSync — not directly to EC2

cards.q: AWS WAF vs AWS Shield: what's the difference?
cards.a: Shield — DDoS (L3/L4, Advanced also L7); WAF — HTTP rule filtering

cards.q: AWS WAF vs AWS Network Firewall: what's the difference?
cards.a: Network Firewall — L3–L7 in the VPC; WAF — HTTP only, in front of the app

cards.q: AWS WAF vs Security Groups: what's the difference?
cards.a: SG — stateful L4 allow-only; can't do SQLi/XSS

cards.q: What is AWS Shield?
cards.a: DDoS protection: Standard is free, Advanced is extended

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“DDoS protection: Standard is free, Advanced is extended”
cards.a: AWS Shield

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Shield?
cards.a:
• DDoS protection for a critical application
• Need SRT support and cost reimbursement during an attack

cards.q: AWS Shield: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Shield Standard — automatic and free, L3/L4
• Shield Advanced: ~$3000/month per organization, 24/7 Shield Response Team
• Advanced: cost protection against bill spikes caused by DDoS
• Protects EC2 EIPs, ELB, CloudFront, Global Accelerator, Route 53

cards.q: When is AWS Shield NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Doesn't replace WAF for SQLi/XSS

cards.q: AWS Shield vs AWS WAF: what's the difference?
cards.a: WAF — L7 rules; Shield — DDoS protection

cards.q: AWS Shield vs AWS Firewall Manager: what's the difference?
cards.a: Firewall Manager centralizes Shield Advanced and WAF across accounts

cards.q: What is AWS Firewall Manager?
cards.a: Centralized WAF/Shield/SG/Network Firewall rules across accounts

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Centralized WAF/Shield/SG/Network Firewall rules across accounts”
cards.a: AWS Firewall Manager

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Firewall Manager?
cards.a:
• Uniform WAF rules for all accounts in the organization
• New resources must get protection automatically

cards.q: AWS Firewall Manager: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Requires Organizations and AWS Config
• Automatically applies policies to new accounts and resources
• Manages WAF, Shield Advanced, Security Groups, Network Firewall, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall

cards.q: When is AWS Firewall Manager NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • For a single account/resource, WAF directly is enough

cards.q: AWS Firewall Manager vs AWS WAF: what's the difference?
cards.a: WAF — the rules themselves; Firewall Manager — rolling them out across the organization

cards.q: What is AWS Network Firewall?
cards.a: Managed stateful firewall/IPS for VPC (L3–L7)

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Managed stateful firewall/IPS for VPC (L3–L7)”
cards.a: AWS Network Firewall

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Network Firewall?
cards.a:
• "Layered / defense-in-depth beyond SGs and NACLs", "block malicious URLs", "drop blacklisted FQDNs" → Network Firewall
• Traffic inspection and filtering at the VPC level
• Allow egress only to specific domains
• IDS/IPS for a VPC

cards.q: AWS Network Firewall: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Deployed into dedicated firewall subnets; you change VPC route tables to send traffic through the firewall endpoints (it does not attach to an ALB)
• Stateful/stateless rules, Suricata-compatible IPS rules, domain filtering
• Stateful domain-list rules (allow/deny FQDNs), Suricata IPS rules, managed threat lists; centralized inspection via Transit Gateway
• Protects all VPC traffic (ingress/egress, VPC-to-VPC)

cards.q: When is AWS Network Firewall NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • For SQLi/XSS in front of a web app, WAF is simpler

cards.q: AWS Network Firewall vs AWS WAF: what's the difference?
cards.a: WAF — HTTP on ALB/CloudFront; Network Firewall — all VPC traffic

cards.q: AWS Network Firewall vs Network ACLs: what's the difference?
cards.a: NACL — stateless by IP/port per subnet; Network Firewall — deep inspection

cards.q: What is Amazon GuardDuty?
cards.a: ML threat detection from logs (CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS)

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“ML threat detection from logs (CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS)”
cards.a: Amazon GuardDuty

cards.q: When would you choose Amazon GuardDuty?
cards.a:
• Continuous threat detection with LEAST operational overhead
• Detect crypto-mining / suspicious API calls
• "Alert on unauthorized access / suspicious access patterns / malicious activity on S3" → GuardDuty S3 Protection

cards.q: Amazon GuardDuty: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Analyzes CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs — without you enabling the logs
• Protection plans: S3 Protection (suspicious S3 access via CloudTrail S3 data events), EKS, RDS login, Lambda, Runtime Monitoring, Malware Protection
• Findings → EventBridge → Lambda/SNS for automated response
• Detects crypto-mining, compromised credentials, communication with malicious IPs
• Multi-account via delegated administrator

cards.q: When is Amazon GuardDuty NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Doesn't scan software vulnerabilities (that's Inspector)
• Doesn't look for PII in S3 (that's Macie)

cards.q: Amazon GuardDuty vs Amazon Inspector: what's the difference?
cards.a: Inspector — vulnerabilities (CVEs); GuardDuty — active threats

cards.q: Amazon GuardDuty vs Amazon Macie: what's the difference?
cards.a: Macie — sensitive data in S3

cards.q: Amazon GuardDuty vs Amazon Detective: what's the difference?
cards.a: Detective — root-cause investigation after GuardDuty findings

cards.q: What is Amazon Inspector?
cards.a: Automated vulnerability scanning of EC2, ECR images, Lambda

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Automated vulnerability scanning of EC2, ECR images, Lambda”
cards.a: Amazon Inspector

cards.q: When would you choose Amazon Inspector?
cards.a:
• Find software vulnerabilities on EC2 / in container images
• Continuous CVE assessment

cards.q: Amazon Inspector: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Scans for CVEs in packages and network reachability
• EC2 via SSM Agent (or agentless), images in ECR, Lambda functions
• Continuous scanning, risk score
• Findings go to Security Hub and EventBridge

cards.q: When is Amazon Inspector NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Doesn't detect attacks from logs (that's GuardDuty)
• Doesn't monitor S3 access — only EC2/ECR/Lambda vulnerabilities

cards.q: Amazon Inspector vs Amazon GuardDuty: what's the difference?
cards.a: GuardDuty — threats from logs; Inspector — software vulnerabilities

cards.q: What is Amazon Macie?
cards.a: ML discovery of sensitive data (PII) in S3

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“ML discovery of sensitive data (PII) in S3”
cards.a: Amazon Macie

cards.q: When would you choose Amazon Macie?
cards.a:
• Find PII/card numbers in S3 buckets
• Compliance: where sensitive data resides

cards.q: Amazon Macie: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Detects PII, financial data, credentials in S3 objects
• Assesses bucket security (public, unencrypted)
• Findings → EventBridge / Security Hub
• S3 only

cards.q: When is Amazon Macie NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Doesn't work with RDS/EBS directly

cards.q: Amazon Macie vs Amazon GuardDuty: what's the difference?
cards.a: GuardDuty — threats; Macie — data classification in S3

cards.q: What is AWS Security Hub?
cards.a: Single pane for security findings and best-practice checks

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Single pane for security findings and best-practice checks”
cards.a: AWS Security Hub

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Security Hub?
cards.a:
• Centralized view of security posture across all accounts
• Automated CIS compliance checks

cards.q: AWS Security Hub: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Firewall Manager, partners
• Standards checks: AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS, PCI DSS
• Requires AWS Config
• Cross-account and cross-Region aggregation

cards.q: When is AWS Security Hub NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Doesn't detect threats from logs itself — it aggregates
• Aggregates findings; doesn't create accounts or baselines

cards.q: AWS Security Hub vs Amazon GuardDuty: what's the difference?
cards.a: GuardDuty generates findings; Security Hub collects them

cards.q: AWS Security Hub vs AWS Config: what's the difference?
cards.a: Config — resource configurations; Security Hub uses it for checks

cards.q: What is Amazon Detective?
cards.a: Incident investigation: relationship graphs from logs

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Incident investigation: relationship graphs from logs”
cards.a: Amazon Detective

cards.q: When would you choose Amazon Detective?
cards.a:
• Need to investigate and find the root cause of a GuardDuty finding
• After an incident, visualize which resources/IPs were involved

cards.q: Amazon Detective: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Builds a graph from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, GuardDuty findings, EKS audit logs
• Helps find the root cause
• Visualizes activity over a time period

cards.q: When is Amazon Detective NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Doesn't detect threats on its own

cards.q: Amazon Detective vs Amazon GuardDuty: what's the difference?
cards.a: GuardDuty finds; Detective investigates

cards.q: What is AWS Artifact?
cards.a: Portal for AWS compliance reports (SOC, PCI, ISO) and agreements

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?

cards.a: AWS Artifact

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Artifact?
cards.a:
• Auditor needs an AWS compliance report (SOC/PCI)
• Sign a BAA

cards.q: AWS Artifact: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Download SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, ISO reports
• Accept agreements (BAA for HIPAA)
• Self-service, no additional charge

cards.q: When is AWS Artifact NOT the right choice?

cards.q: AWS Artifact vs AWS Audit Manager: what's the difference?

cards.q: What is AWS Audit Manager?

cards.q:
Which Security, Identity & Compliance service/concept is this?
“Continuous audit evidence collection for your AWS resources”
cards.a: AWS Audit Manager

cards.q: AWS Audit Manager: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Prebuilt frameworks: GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOC 2
• Automatically collects evidence from Config, CloudTrail, Security Hub
• Generates reports for auditors

cards.q: When is AWS Audit Manager NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Doesn't provide compliance reports about AWS itself (that's Artifact)

cards.q: AWS Audit Manager vs AWS Artifact: what's the difference?
cards.a: Artifact — AWS reports; Audit Manager — evidence about your environment

cards.q: AWS Audit Manager vs AWS Config: what's the difference?

cards.q: What is Amazon VPC?
cards.a: Isolated virtual network in a Region

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Isolated virtual network in a Region”
cards.a: Amazon VPC

cards.q: When would you choose Amazon VPC?
cards.a:
• Isolate resources in your own network
• Separate public/private tiers

cards.q: Amazon VPC: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Regional; spans all AZs of the Region, subnets live in a single AZ
• CIDR from /16 to /28; secondary CIDRs can be added
• Default VPC in every Region (public subnets)
• IPv6 dual-stack supported; up to 5 VPCs per Region (soft limit)
• Route tables, IGW, NAT, endpoints, SG, NACL — the building blocks

cards.q: When is Amazon VPC NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • VPCs with overlapping CIDRs can't be peered

cards.q: Amazon VPC vs VPC Peering: what's the difference?
cards.a: Peering connects two VPCs; the VPC is the network itself

cards.q: Amazon VPC vs AWS Transit Gateway: what's the difference?
cards.a: TGW — hub for many VPCs and on-prem

cards.q: What is Subnets & Route Tables?
cards.a: IP range in one AZ; public or private depending on the route table

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“IP range in one AZ; public or private depending on the route table”
cards.a: Subnets & Route Tables

cards.q: When would you choose Subnets & Route Tables?
cards.a:
• Split tiers: ALB in public, app and DB in private
• Multi-AZ deployment

cards.q: Subnets & Route Tables: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Subnet = one AZ
• AWS reserves 5 IPs in every subnet (first 4 and the last)
• Every route table has an implicit local route (VPC CIDR → local): all subnets in a VPC reach each other without IGW/NAT
• Public = route 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW; private — without it
• For HA — subnets in at least 2 AZs

cards.q:
Subnets & Route Tables — fill in the blank:
For HA — subnets in at least _____
cards.a:
2 AZs

For HA — subnets in at least 2 AZs

cards.q: When is Subnets & Route Tables NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• A /28 subnet gives only 11 usable IPs — a calculation trap
• Intra-VPC connectivity problems are never fixed by NAT/IGW routes — check SGs and NACLs

cards.q: Subnets & Route Tables vs Network ACLs: what's the difference?
cards.a: NACL applies at the subnet level

cards.q: What is Security Groups?
cards.a: Stateful firewall at the ENI/instance level, allow only

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Stateful firewall at the ENI/instance level, allow only”
cards.a: Security Groups

cards.q: When would you choose Security Groups?
cards.a:
• Allow the DB to accept traffic only from the app's SG
• Access control at the instance level
• Bastion pattern: bastion SG allows SSH/RDP only from corporate IPs; instance SGs allow it only from the bastion SG

cards.q: Security Groups: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Stateful: return traffic is allowed automatically
• Allow rules only, no deny
• Source can be another SG (SG reference)
• Default: all inbound denied, all outbound allowed
• All rules are evaluated

cards.q: When is Security Groups NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Can't block a specific IP (no deny) → NACL or WAF

cards.q: Security Groups vs Network ACLs: what's the difference?
cards.a: NACL — stateless, subnet-level, has deny and rule ordering

cards.q: Security Groups vs AWS WAF: what's the difference?
cards.a: WAF — L7 rules for HTTP

cards.q: What is Network ACLs?
cards.a: Stateless firewall at the subnet level, allow and deny

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Stateless firewall at the subnet level, allow and deny”
cards.a: Network ACLs

cards.q: When would you choose Network ACLs?
cards.a:
• Block a specific IP/range at the subnet level
• Additional layer of subnet protection
• Two subnets in one VPC can't talk → check NACLs of both subnets (+ SGs)

cards.q: Network ACLs: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Stateless: return traffic must be explicitly allowed (ephemeral ports 1024–65535)
• Rules by number, first match wins
• Has deny — can block specific IPs
• Default NACL allows everything; a custom one denies everything by default

cards.q: When is Network ACLs NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Forgetting ephemeral ports in outbound is a common cause of broken connectivity

cards.q: Network ACLs vs Security Groups: what's the difference?
cards.a: SG — stateful, instance, allow only; NACL — stateless, subnet, allow+deny

cards.q: Network ACLs vs AWS Network Firewall: what's the difference?
cards.a: Network Firewall — deep inspection; NACL — simple IP/port rules

cards.q: What is Internet Gateway?
cards.a: Internet Gateway: VPC access to the internet (both directions)

cards.q: When would you choose Internet Gateway?
cards.a:
• Make a subnet public
• Instances must be reachable from the internet

cards.q: Internet Gateway: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• One IGW per VPC, horizontally scaled, HA
• Instance needs a public IP/Elastic IP + route 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW
• Egress-only IGW — outbound IPv6 with no inbound

cards.q: When is Internet Gateway NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • A private subnet must not have a route to the IGW — use NAT for outbound

cards.q: Internet Gateway vs NAT Gateway: what's the difference?
cards.a: NAT — outbound-only IPv4 from a private subnet; IGW — bidirectional

cards.q: What is NAT Gateway?
cards.a: Managed NAT: outbound internet for private subnets

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Managed NAT: outbound internet for private subnets”
cards.a: NAT Gateway

cards.q: When would you choose NAT Gateway?
cards.a:
• Private instances need updates from the internet without inbound access
• Replace a NAT instance with LEAST operational overhead

cards.q: NAT Gateway: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Placed in a public subnet, needs an Elastic IP (public NAT)
• Zonal: for HA — one NAT Gateway per AZ
• Up to 100 Gbps, managed; NAT instance — legacy self-managed alternative
• Charged per hour + per GB processed — expensive with heavy traffic to S3
• Doesn't support SGs

cards.q:
NAT Gateway — fill in the blank:
Up to _____, managed; NAT instance — legacy self-managed alternative
cards.a:
100 Gbps

Up to 100 Gbps, managed; NAT instance — legacy self-managed alternative

cards.q: When is NAT Gateway NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Traffic to S3/DynamoDB through NAT is expensive — use a Gateway endpoint
• One NAT for all AZs — single point of failure
• Doesn't filter domains/URLs — it only gives private subnets outbound internet

cards.q: NAT Gateway vs Internet Gateway: what's the difference?
cards.a: IGW — bidirectional access for public; NAT — outbound only

cards.q: NAT Gateway vs VPC Endpoints (Gateway / Interface): what's the difference?
cards.a: Gateway endpoint to S3/DynamoDB is free and needs no NAT

cards.q: What is Bastion Host (jump box)?
cards.a: Hardened EC2 in a public subnet used as the only admin entry point

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Hardened EC2 in a public subnet used as the only admin entry point”
cards.a: Bastion Host (jump box)

cards.q: When would you choose Bastion Host (jump box)?
cards.a:
• "Limit administrative access to instances in private subnets over the Internet"
• Company has no VPN/DX to the VPC and needs RDP/SSH admin access

cards.q: Bastion Host (jump box): what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Lives in a public subnet with a public/Elastic IP
• Bastion SG: SSH 22 (Linux) / RDP 3389 (Windows) only from corporate public IP ranges
• Instance SGs: allow SSH/RDP only from the bastion's SG (SG reference)
• Make it HA with an Auto Scaling group across AZs
• Modern alternative: SSM Session Manager — no bastion, no open ports, audited

cards.q: When is Bastion Host (jump box) NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Private subnet bastion — unreachable from the Internet even with an EIP
• Opening SSH/RDP from 0.0.0.0/0
• LEAST operational overhead / no open ports → Session Manager

cards.q: Bastion Host (jump box) vs AWS Systems Manager: what's the difference?
cards.a: Session Manager replaces bastions: no inbound ports, IAM-controlled, logged

cards.q: Bastion Host (jump box) vs Security Groups: what's the difference?
cards.a: SG reference: instances trust only the bastion's SG

cards.q: What is VPC Endpoints (Gateway / Interface)?
cards.a: Private access to AWS services without IGW/NAT

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Private access to AWS services without IGW/NAT”
cards.a: VPC Endpoints (Gateway / Interface)

cards.q: When would you choose VPC Endpoints (Gateway / Interface)?
cards.a:
• Private subnet → S3 without internet and at minimal cost → Gateway endpoint
• Access to SQS/KMS/SSM from a private subnet without NAT → Interface endpoint
• Allow a bucket only from a specific VPC endpoint
• "VPC may reach only trusted buckets via the gateway endpoint" → endpoint policy listing those buckets

cards.q: VPC Endpoints (Gateway / Interface): what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Gateway endpoint: S3 and DynamoDB, added as a target in route tables (prefix list), free — the default exam answer for private S3/DynamoDB access
• Interface endpoint (PrivateLink): ENI with a private IP, most services, paid
• Interface endpoint is reachable from on-prem via VPN/DX; Gateway is not
• Endpoint policy = what can be reached THROUGH the endpoint (e.g. only trusted bucket ARNs); bucket policy with aws:SourceVpce/aws:SourceVpc = who may reach the bucket

cards.q: When is VPC Endpoints (Gateway / Interface) NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Gateway endpoint doesn't work from on-prem or from a peered VPC
• Interface endpoints are ENIs in subnets (private DNS) — they are not "associated with route tables"; NACLs filter CIDRs, not endpoint DNS names

cards.q: VPC Endpoints (Gateway / Interface) vs NAT Gateway: what's the difference?
cards.a: NAT is charged per GB; Gateway endpoint for S3 is free

cards.q: VPC Endpoints (Gateway / Interface) vs AWS PrivateLink: what's the difference?
cards.a: Interface endpoint is built on PrivateLink

cards.q: What is AWS PrivateLink?
cards.a: Private access to a service in another VPC/account via ENI

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Private access to a service in another VPC/account via ENI”
cards.a: AWS PrivateLink

cards.q: When would you choose AWS PrivateLink?
cards.a:
• Expose a service to hundreds of customer VPCs without peering
• CIDRs overlap, peering impossible
• Access to only one application, not the whole network

cards.q: AWS PrivateLink: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Provider: NLB (or GWLB) + endpoint service; consumer: interface endpoint
• One-way access to a specific service, not the whole VPC
• Works with overlapping CIDRs
• Scales to thousands of consumers (SaaS)

cards.q: When is AWS PrivateLink NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Not for full connectivity between VPCs (that's peering/TGW)

cards.q: AWS PrivateLink vs VPC Peering: what's the difference?
cards.a: Peering — whole network, no CIDR overlap; PrivateLink — one service, overlap OK

cards.q: AWS PrivateLink vs AWS Transit Gateway: what's the difference?
cards.a: TGW — transitive routing across many networks

cards.q: What is VPC Peering?
cards.a: Direct connection of two VPCs (incl. cross-account/Region)

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Direct connection of two VPCs (incl. cross-account/Region)”
cards.a: VPC Peering

cards.q: When would you choose VPC Peering?
cards.a:
• Connect a few VPCs cheaply and simply
• Cross-account access between two VPCs

cards.q: VPC Peering: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Non-transitive: A↔B and B↔C don't give A↔C
• DEV↔UAT + UAT↔PROD ≠ DEV↔PROD: create a direct DEV↔PROD peering + routes both ways
• CIDRs must not overlap
• Routes needed in route tables on both sides
• No charge for the connection; inter-AZ/Region traffic is paid
• No edge-to-edge routing (via the peer's IGW/VPN)

cards.q: When is VPC Peering NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Many VPCs (full mesh) → Transit Gateway
• Overlapping CIDRs → PrivateLink
• On-prem reaching VPC-A through VPC-B's VPN/DX/IGW — impossible (no edge-to-edge routing)

cards.q: VPC Peering vs AWS Transit Gateway: what's the difference?
cards.a: TGW — hub-and-spoke, transitive, for tens/hundreds of VPCs

cards.q: VPC Peering vs AWS PrivateLink: what's the difference?
cards.a: PrivateLink — access to one service, allows CIDR overlap

cards.q: What is AWS Transit Gateway?
cards.a: Regional hub connecting thousands of VPCs and on-prem (transitively)

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Regional hub connecting thousands of VPCs and on-prem (transitively)”
cards.a: AWS Transit Gateway

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Transit Gateway?
cards.a:
• Many VPCs + on-prem, simplify a complex peering mesh
• Increase VPN throughput (ECMP)

cards.q: AWS Transit Gateway: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Hub-and-spoke, transitive routing
• Attaches VPCs, VPN, Direct Connect (via DX Gateway)
• Inter-Region peering between TGWs; sharing via RAM
• TGW route tables for segmentation
• ECMP across multiple VPN tunnels to increase throughput

cards.q: When is AWS Transit Gateway NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • For 2–3 VPCs, peering is cheaper

cards.q: AWS Transit Gateway vs VPC Peering: what's the difference?
cards.a: Peering — point-to-point, non-transitive; TGW — central hub

cards.q: AWS Transit Gateway vs AWS Direct Connect: what's the difference?
cards.a: DX attaches to TGW via Direct Connect Gateway (transit VIF)

cards.q: What is AWS Site-to-Site VPN?
cards.a: IPsec VPN between on-prem and AWS over the internet

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“IPsec VPN between on-prem and AWS over the internet”
cards.a: AWS Site-to-Site VPN

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Site-to-Site VPN?
cards.a:
• Connect on-prem quickly (days/hours)
• Encrypted backup link for Direct Connect
• Encryption over Direct Connect

cards.q: AWS Site-to-Site VPN: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• VGW or TGW on the AWS side; on-prem: Customer Gateway device with a static, Internet-routable public IP (behind NAT only with NAT-T)
• 2 tunnels for redundancy; ~1.25 Gbps per tunnel
• Set up in minutes, cheaper than Direct Connect
• IPsec encryption; can be a backup for DX
• VPN CloudHub — connecting multiple offices via VGW
• VPC side: route to the VGW (or enable route propagation); VGW tunnel endpoints are AWS-managed — no Elastic IP to attach

cards.q:
AWS Site-to-Site VPN — fill in the blank:
2 tunnels for redundancy; ~_____ per tunnel
cards.a:
1.25 Gbps

2 tunnels for redundancy; ~1.25 Gbps per tunnel

cards.q: When is AWS Site-to-Site VPN NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Need consistent latency/high throughput → Direct Connect
• VPN CloudHub does not create Direct Connect connections — it's hub-and-spoke VPN between branch sites
• NAT instance/Gateway or an EIP on the VGW are never VPN requirements

cards.q: AWS Site-to-Site VPN vs AWS Direct Connect: what's the difference?
cards.a: DX — dedicated link, consistent, but slow to set up (weeks) and unencrypted by default

cards.q: AWS Site-to-Site VPN vs AWS Client VPN: what's the difference?
cards.a: Client VPN — for individual users, not for a network

cards.q: What is AWS Client VPN?
cards.a: Managed OpenVPN user access to VPC/on-prem

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Managed OpenVPN user access to VPC/on-prem”
cards.a: AWS Client VPN

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Client VPN?
cards.a:
• Remote employees must connect securely to private resources
• Employee access to on-prem via a VPC connected over VPN/DX

cards.q: AWS Client VPN: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Clients use OpenVPN-compatible software
• Authentication: AD, SAML, certificates (mutual TLS)
• Associated with VPC subnets

cards.q: When is AWS Client VPN NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Not for connecting office networks (that's Site-to-Site VPN)

cards.q: AWS Client VPN vs AWS Site-to-Site VPN: what's the difference?
cards.a: S2S — network to network; Client VPN — user's laptop to VPC

cards.q: What is AWS Direct Connect?
cards.a: Dedicated private link from on-prem to AWS

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Dedicated private link from on-prem to AWS”
cards.a: AWS Direct Connect

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Direct Connect?
cards.a:
• Consistent latency and high throughput
• Large recurring data volumes, reduce egress cost
• Private connection without the internet

cards.q: AWS Direct Connect: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Dedicated 1/10/100 Gbps or Hosted from 50 Mbps to 25 Gbps via a partner
• Provisioning takes weeks
• Not encrypted by default → VPN over DX or MACsec
• VIF: private (VPC), public (AWS public services), transit (TGW)
• Direct Connect Gateway — access to VPCs in different Regions
• HA: two DX connections in different locations; cheap option — DX + VPN backup

cards.q:
AWS Direct Connect — fill in the blank:
Dedicated 1/10/_____ or Hosted from 50 Mbps to 25 Gbps via a partner
cards.a:
100 Gbps

Dedicated 1/10/100 Gbps or Hosted from 50 Mbps to 25 Gbps via a partner

cards.q: When is AWS Direct Connect NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Need to connect urgently — DX takes long; use VPN temporarily
• Encryption is not enabled by default
• A DX/VPN into a peered VPC gives no resiliency for the other VPC — the backup must terminate on the same VPC (or use TGW / DX Gateway)

cards.q: AWS Direct Connect vs AWS Site-to-Site VPN: what's the difference?
cards.a: VPN — fast and encrypted over the internet; DX — consistent, dedicated, slow to provision

cards.q: AWS Direct Connect vs AWS Transit Gateway: what's the difference?
cards.a: Transit VIF + DX Gateway connect DX to TGW

cards.q: What is VPC Flow Logs?
cards.a: IP traffic metadata logs for VPC/subnet/ENI

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“IP traffic metadata logs for VPC/subnet/ENI”
cards.a: VPC Flow Logs

cards.q: When would you choose VPC Flow Logs?
cards.a:
• Troubleshooting: why traffic is blocked (SG/NACL)
• Auditing network connections

cards.q: VPC Flow Logs: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Delivered to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose
• Metadata (src/dst IP, port, ACCEPT/REJECT), not packet contents
• Levels: VPC, subnet, ENI
• Analysis via Athena or CloudWatch Logs Insights

cards.q: When is VPC Flow Logs NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Don't capture payload — that's Traffic Mirroring

cards.q: VPC Flow Logs vs AWS CloudTrail: what's the difference?
cards.a: CloudTrail — API calls; Flow Logs — network traffic

cards.q: VPC Flow Logs vs Amazon GuardDuty: what's the difference?
cards.a: GuardDuty analyzes flow logs automatically

cards.q: What is Elastic Load Balancing (ALB / NLB / GWLB)?
cards.a: Load balancers: ALB (L7), NLB (L4), GWLB (L3)

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Load balancers: ALB (L7), NLB (L4), GWLB (L3)”
cards.a: Elastic Load Balancing (ALB / NLB / GWLB)

cards.q: When would you choose Elastic Load Balancing (ALB / NLB / GWLB)?
cards.a:
• Routing by URL path/hostname, microservices → ALB
• Clients must whitelist the endpoint's IPs on their firewall → NLB with an Elastic IP per AZ
• Need static IP, TCP/UDP, extreme performance → NLB
• Route traffic through a third-party firewall → GWLB

cards.q: Elastic Load Balancing (ALB / NLB / GWLB): what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• ALB: HTTP/HTTPS, path/host/header routing, targets EC2/IP/Lambda, WAF, auth via Cognito
• NLB: TCP/UDP/TLS, millions of rps, ultra-low latency, static IP / Elastic IP per AZ
• GWLB: proxy for third-party appliances (firewall, IDS), GENEVE 6081
• Health checks; cross-zone balancing (on by default for ALB)
• Sticky sessions, SSL termination via ACM, SNI
• Connection draining (deregistration delay)

cards.q: When is Elastic Load Balancing (ALB / NLB / GWLB) NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• WAF can't be attached to NLB
• ALB doesn't provide a static IP (put an NLB in front of ALB, or Global Accelerator)
• Elastic IP on an ALB — impossible; ALB IPs change as it scales

cards.q: Elastic Load Balancing (ALB / NLB / GWLB) vs AWS Global Accelerator: what's the difference?
cards.a: GA — global anycast IPs and cross-Region routing; ELB — within one Region

cards.q: Elastic Load Balancing (ALB / NLB / GWLB) vs Amazon API Gateway: what's the difference?
cards.a: API Gateway — API management (throttling, keys); ALB — simple load balancing

cards.q: Elastic Load Balancing (ALB / NLB / GWLB) vs Amazon Route 53: what's the difference?
cards.a: Route 53 — DNS-level balancing across Regions

cards.q: What is Amazon Route 53?
cards.a: Managed DNS, domain registration and routing policies

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Managed DNS, domain registration and routing policies”
cards.a: Amazon Route 53

cards.q: When would you choose Amazon Route 53?
cards.a:
• Active-passive failover between Regions
• Route users to the lowest-latency Region
• Content by user's country (geolocation)
• Blue/green, canary via weighted

cards.q: Amazon Route 53: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Routing: simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation, geoproximity, multivalue, IP-based
• Geolocation = WHERE the user is (country/continent → fixed endpoint, all-or-nothing); Geoproximity = HOW FAR (nearest resource, bias −99..+99 grows/shrinks a Region's area — "shift a larger portion")
• Alias record — free, works at the zone apex, points to AWS resources (ELB, CloudFront, S3)
• CNAME not allowed at the zone apex
• Failover routing: primary record + health check, secondary → DR; Evaluate Target Health (alias to ELB) inherits target health; health checkers must be allowed by NACL/SG
• Private hosted zones for VPC; Resolver endpoints for hybrid DNS

cards.q: When is Amazon Route 53 NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• DNS failover depends on TTL and client caching — not instant (GA is faster)
• Geolocation can't send a 'larger portion' — it maps whole locations; proportional shift = geoproximity bias, % split for everyone = weighted
• Weighted routing for "DR only on outage" — weighted always splits traffic; custom Lambda calling ChangeResourceRecordSets — reinvents failover routing

cards.q: Amazon Route 53 vs AWS Global Accelerator: what's the difference?
cards.a: GA — anycast IPs, failover in seconds without DNS caching

cards.q: Amazon Route 53 vs Elastic Load Balancing (ALB / NLB / GWLB): what's the difference?
cards.a: ELB — within a Region; Route 53 — across Regions

cards.q: Amazon Route 53 vs Amazon CloudFront: what's the difference?
cards.a: CloudFront caches content; Route 53 only resolves names

cards.q: What is Amazon CloudFront?
cards.a: Global CDN: caching at edge locations

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Global CDN: caching at edge locations”
cards.a: Amazon CloudFront

cards.q: When would you choose Amazon CloudFront?
cards.a:
• Reduce latency for static/dynamic content worldwide
• Serve private S3 content only via the CDN (OAC)
• Reduce load on the origin
• "Static content to users worldwide, reduce server costs, secure" → S3 origin + CloudFront (no servers at all)

cards.q: Amazon CloudFront: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Origins: S3, ALB, EC2, any HTTP; Origin Access Control (OAC) for private S3
• Signed URLs / signed cookies for private content
• Geo restriction, WAF, Shield; HTTPS with an ACM certificate from us-east-1
• Cache behaviors by path, TTL, invalidation
• Lambda@Edge (viewer/origin request+response, can rewrite URI by User-Agent, full Node/Python) vs CloudFront Functions (viewer events only, ultra-light header/URL logic)
• Origin failover via origin groups

cards.q: When is Amazon CloudFront NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Not for non-HTTP protocols (TCP/UDP games) → Global Accelerator
• Custom origin on private IPs of web servers — origin must be publicly reachable; CloudFront edge IPs aren't a fixed whitelistable set
• Route 53 can't route by HTTP headers (User-Agent) — that's CloudFront/Lambda@Edge logic

cards.q: Amazon CloudFront vs AWS Global Accelerator: what's the difference?
cards.a: GA — TCP/UDP, no caching, static anycast IPs; CloudFront — HTTP cache

cards.q: Amazon CloudFront vs Amazon S3: what's the difference?
cards.a: S3 Transfer Acceleration — faster uploads to S3; CloudFront — content delivery

cards.q: What is AWS Global Accelerator?
cards.a: Anycast static IPs and routing over the AWS network to the nearest Region

cards.q:
Which Networking & Content Delivery service/concept is this?
“Anycast static IPs and routing over the AWS network to the nearest Region”
cards.a: AWS Global Accelerator

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Global Accelerator?
cards.a:

• Need fixed IPs for customer whitelisting
• Fast regional failover without DNS TTL
• HTTP only when it specifically needs static IPs or deterministic, fast regional failover

cards.q: AWS Global Accelerator: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• 2 static anycast IPs per application
• Endpoints: ALB, NLB, EC2, Elastic IP in one or many Regions
• Health checks, failover in < 1 minute, no DNS caching
• TCP and UDP, no caching

1 minute

• Static files / S3 — GA can't use S3 as an endpoint and doesn't cache

cards.q: AWS Global Accelerator vs Amazon CloudFront: what's the difference?
cards.a: CloudFront — HTTP cache at the edge; GA — TCP/UDP proxy with static IPs, no cache

cards.q: AWS Global Accelerator vs Amazon Route 53: what's the difference?

cards.q: What is Amazon EC2?
cards.a: Virtual servers (instances) with full OS control

cards.q:
Which Compute service/concept is this?
“Virtual servers (instances) with full OS control”
cards.a: Amazon EC2

cards.q: When would you choose Amazon EC2?
cards.a:
• Need full control of OS/software, legacy applications
• Long-running workloads, specific hardware (GPU)
• "Keep the same private IP and fail over to another instance" → move a secondary ENI

cards.q: Amazon EC2: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Families: general (M, T), compute (C), memory (R, X), storage (I, D), accelerated (P, G, Inf)
• T instances are burstable (CPU credits)
• User data — script at first boot; instance metadata 169.254.169.254 (IMDSv2)
• Role via instance profile, not access keys
• Stop/start changes the host and public IP (except Elastic IP); hibernate saves RAM to EBS
• ENI: secondary ENIs keep private IP/MAC/SGs and can be moved to another instance in the same AZ (failover); the primary ENI (eth0) can't be detached

cards.q: When is Amazon EC2 NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• If LEAST operational overhead is required — Lambda/Fargate/Beanstalk are often better
• Elastic IP for a private-IP endpoint — EIPs are public addresses

cards.q: Amazon EC2 vs AWS Lambda: what's the difference?
cards.a: Lambda — serverless, up to 15 min; EC2 — full control and any duration

cards.q: Amazon EC2 vs AWS Fargate: what's the difference?
cards.a: Fargate — containers without managing instances

cards.q: When would you choose EC2 Purchasing Options (On-Demand / RI / Savings Plans / Spot)?
cards.a:
• Steady 24/7 workload for years → RI / Savings Plans
• Interruptible batch/CI jobs, stateless → Spot
• Per-socket/per-core licenses (BYOL) → Dedicated Hosts
• Guarantee capacity for an event → Capacity Reservation

cards.q: EC2 Purchasing Options (On-Demand / RI / Savings Plans / Spot): what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• On-Demand — no commitment, for short unpredictable workloads
• Reserved Instances / Savings Plans — 1 or 3 years, up to ~72% discount
• Compute Savings Plans are more flexible (any family/Region, Fargate, Lambda); EC2 Instance SP — family+Region
• Spot — up to 90% discount, can be interrupted with a 2-min notice
• Dedicated Hosts — socket/core-level BYOL, compliance; Dedicated Instances — hardware isolation
• Capacity Reservations — guaranteed capacity in an AZ, no discount

cards.q: What is EC2 Auto Scaling?

Which Compute service/concept is this?
“Auto Scaling Group: automatic EC2 count based on load and health”
cards.a: EC2 Auto Scaling

cards.q: When would you choose EC2 Auto Scaling?
cards.a:
• Keep CPU at ~50% → target tracking
• Known peak on a schedule → scheduled scaling
• Self-healing when an instance fails
• Predictable load cycles → predictive scaling

cards.q: EC2 Auto Scaling: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Min/desired/max; launch template
• Policies: target tracking (simplest), step, simple, scheduled, predictive

cards.q: When is EC2 Auto Scaling NOT the right choice?

cards.q: AWS Batch: what are the key exam facts?

• Automatically selects and scales capacity

cards.q: S3 Security (Bucket Policy, Block Public Access, Object Lock, Encryption): what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Default encryption SSE-S3; also SSE-KMS, DSSE-KMS, SSE-C, client-side
• Headers: `x-amz-server-side-encryption: AES256` (SSE-S3) or `aws:kms` (+ `-aws-kms-key-id`) for SSE-KMS; SSE-C uses `-customer-algorithm`, `-customer-key`, `-customer-key-MD5` on every request
• Block Public Access (on by default), bucket policy, IAM
• Object Ownership: ACLs disabled by default (bucket owner enforced)
• aws:SecureTransport to enforce HTTPS; MFA Delete
• Object Lock (requires versioning): Compliance = nobody, not even root, can delete/shorten retention; Governance = users with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention can; legal hold = no expiry

• Headers containing `-customer-` are SSE-C only — never the answer for SSE-S3/SSE-KMS

“Serverless SQL queries directly against data in S3”
cards.a: Amazon Athena

cards.q: When would you choose Amazon Athena?
cards.a:
• Ad-hoc SQL analysis of logs in S3 (CloudTrail, ALB, VPC Flow Logs)
• One-off queries with no data loading or infrastructure

cards.q: Amazon Athena: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Pay per data scanned (~$5 per TB)
• Optimization: Parquet/ORC, compression, partitioning → less data scanned
• Uses the Glue Data Catalog
• Federated queries to other sources via Lambda connectors

cards.q: When is Amazon Athena NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Frequent, complex, high-performance BI queries → Redshift

cards.q: Amazon Athena vs Amazon Redshift: what's the difference?
cards.a: Redshift — data warehouse for frequent complex queries; Athena — serverless ad-hoc on S3

cards.q: Amazon Athena vs Amazon EMR: what's the difference?
cards.a: EMR — Spark/Hadoop clusters for heavy processing

cards.q: Amazon Athena vs AWS Glue: what's the difference?
cards.a: Glue Catalog stores schemas for Athena

cards.q: What is AWS Glue?
cards.a: Serverless ETL and Data Catalog

cards.q:
Which Analytics & Streaming service/concept is this?
“Serverless ETL and Data Catalog”
cards.a: AWS Glue

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Glue?
cards.a:
• Serverless ETL: convert CSV to Parquet (crawler discovers schema + scheduled/triggered ETL job)
• Catalog S3 data for Athena
• Data integration with LEAST operational overhead

cards.q: AWS Glue: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Glue ETL jobs on Spark (Python/Scala), serverless
• Crawlers automatically infer schemas and populate the Data Catalog
• Data Catalog is used by Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR
• Job bookmarks — process only new data
• Glue DataBrew — visual data preparation; Glue Data Quality

cards.q: When is AWS Glue NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Long-running, customized Hadoop/Spark clusters → EMR

cards.q: AWS Glue vs Amazon EMR: what's the difference?
cards.a: EMR — managed clusters with full control; Glue — serverless ETL

cards.q: AWS Glue vs Amazon Athena: what's the difference?
cards.a: Athena queries data described in the Glue Catalog

cards.q: AWS Glue vs AWS Lake Formation: what's the difference?
cards.a: Lake Formation is built on top of the Glue Catalog and adds permissions

cards.q: What is AWS Lake Formation?
cards.a: Build and govern access to a data lake on S3

cards.q:
Which Analytics & Streaming service/concept is this?
“Build and govern access to a data lake on S3”
cards.a: AWS Lake Formation

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Lake Formation?
cards.a:
• Quickly build a data lake
• Column/row-level access control for Athena/Redshift/EMR

cards.q: AWS Lake Formation: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Centralized fine-grained permissions (column/row/cell level)
• Built on the Glue Data Catalog
• Blueprints for data ingestion; LF-Tags
• Cross-account data sharing

cards.q: AWS Lake Formation vs AWS Glue: what's the difference?
cards.a: Glue — ETL and catalog; Lake Formation — permissions and data lake management

cards.q: What is Amazon Redshift?
cards.a: Columnar data warehouse (OLAP), provisioned or serverless

cards.q:
Which Analytics & Streaming service/concept is this?

cards.a: Amazon Redshift

• Data warehouse with frequent reporting

cards.q: Amazon Redshift: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Columnar storage, MPP, for analytics (OLAP), not OLTP
• Redshift Spectrum — query data in S3 without loading it
• Redshift Serverless; RA3 with managed storage
• Snapshots, cross-region snapshot copy; Multi-AZ for RA3
• Zero-ETL integrations with Aurora/RDS/DynamoDB; concurrency scaling

cards.q: When is Amazon Redshift NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Not for transactional OLTP workloads
• For one-off queries on S3, Athena is cheaper

cards.q: Amazon Redshift vs Amazon Athena: what's the difference?
cards.a: Athena — serverless ad-hoc on S3; Redshift — DWH for ongoing complex queries

cards.q: Amazon Redshift vs Amazon RDS: what's the difference?
cards.a: RDS — OLTP; Redshift — OLAP

cards.q: Amazon Redshift vs Amazon EMR: what's the difference?

cards.a: Amazon EMR

cards.q: When would you choose Amazon EMR?
cards.a:

• Large-scale data processing, ML data preparation

cards.q: Amazon EMR: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Master/core/task nodes; task nodes are a good fit for Spot
• EMR on EC2, EMR on EKS, EMR Serverless
• Storage in HDFS or S3 (EMRFS)

cards.q: When is Amazon EMR NOT the right choice?

cards.q: Amazon EMR vs AWS Glue: what's the difference?

cards.q: Amazon EMR vs Amazon Athena: what's the difference?

• Ingestion via Firehose, OpenSearch Ingestion, Logstash

cards.q: When is Amazon OpenSearch Service NOT the right choice?

cards.q: Amazon OpenSearch Service vs Amazon Athena: what's the difference?

cards.q: Amazon QuickSight: what are the key exam facts?

• Sources: Redshift, Athena, RDS, S3, SaaS

cards.q: Amazon QuickSight vs Amazon Redshift: what's the difference?
cards.a: Redshift stores and computes; QuickSight visualizes

cards.q: Amazon QuickSight vs Amazon OpenSearch Service: what's the difference?
cards.a: OpenSearch Dashboards — for logs/search

cards.q: What is AWS DMS?
cards.a: Database Migration Service: database migration and replication with minimal downtime

cards.q:
Which Migration & Transfer service/concept is this?
“Database Migration Service: database migration and replication with minimal downtime”
cards.a: AWS DMS

cards.q: When would you choose AWS DMS?
cards.a:
• Migrate a database to AWS with minimal downtime
• Continuous replication of an on-prem database to AWS (CDC)
• "Copy the DB, then continually stream ongoing changes" (even into S3) → DMS full load + CDC
• Migrate a self-managed/embedded NoSQL DB (e.g. MongoDB) into DynamoDB with ongoing replication

cards.q: AWS DMS: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Source stays available during migration
• Homogeneous (Oracle→Oracle) and heterogeneous (Oracle→Aurora, requires schema conversion)
• CDC — continuous replication of changes
• Replication instance or DMS Serverless; Multi-AZ
• Targets: RDS, Aurora, Redshift, DynamoDB, S3, OpenSearch, Kinesis
• Task types: full load, CDC only, full load + CDC; S3 target writes CSV (default) or Parquet; SSL endpoints via imported CA certificate

cards.q: When is AWS DMS NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Does not convert schemas between different engines by itself → SCT / DMS Schema Conversion

cards.q: AWS DMS vs AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT): what's the difference?
cards.a: SCT converts schema/code; DMS moves the data

cards.q: AWS DMS vs AWS DataSync: what's the difference?
cards.a: DataSync — files and objects, not databases

cards.q: What is AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)?
cards.a: Schema Conversion Tool: convert database schema and code between engines

cards.q:
Which Migration & Transfer service/concept is this?
“Schema Conversion Tool: convert database schema and code between engines”
cards.a: AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)?
cards.a:
• Migrate Oracle/SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL/MySQL
• Assess conversion complexity

cards.q: AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT): what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Converts schemas, stored procedures, views
• Required for heterogeneous migration (Oracle → PostgreSQL)
• Also available built-in as DMS Schema Conversion
• Not needed for same-engine migrations

cards.q: When is AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• MySQL → RDS MySQL — SCT not needed
• Doesn't move data or capture changes — it converts schemas/code between engines

cards.q: AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) vs AWS DMS: what's the difference?
cards.a: DMS moves data; SCT converts the schema

cards.q: What is AWS DataSync?
cards.a: Online transfer and sync of files/objects into AWS and between services

cards.q:
Which Migration & Transfer service/concept is this?
“Online transfer and sync of files/objects into AWS and between services”
cards.a: AWS DataSync

cards.q: When would you choose AWS DataSync?
cards.a:
• Move NFS/SMB data to S3/EFS/FSx over the network
• Recurring on-prem → AWS sync
• Copy between EFS/FSx/S3
• "Move historical/cold records off on-prem storage cheaply" → DataSync straight into Glacier Deep Archive (no Standard + lifecycle hop)

cards.q: AWS DataSync: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Sources: NFS, SMB, HDFS, object storage, other clouds
• Destinations: S3 (writes directly into any storage class, incl. Glacier Deep Archive), EFS, FSx
• Agent on-prem; no agent needed between AWS services
• Encryption, integrity verification, preserves metadata/permissions
• Scheduling, bandwidth throttling

cards.q: When is AWS DataSync NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Very large volume over a slow link → Snowball
• Ongoing hybrid access → Storage Gateway
• No database CDC — it copies files/objects, not ongoing DB changes (that's DMS)

cards.q: AWS DataSync vs AWS Storage Gateway: what's the difference?
cards.a: Storage Gateway — ongoing access; DataSync — transfer/sync

cards.q: AWS DataSync vs AWS Snow Family: what's the difference?
cards.a: Snowball — offline, when the network is too slow

cards.q: AWS DataSync vs AWS Transfer Family: what's the difference?
cards.a: Transfer Family — SFTP/FTP endpoint for partners

cards.q: What is AWS Transfer Family?
cards.a: Managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2 server backed by S3 or EFS

cards.q:
Which Migration & Transfer service/concept is this?
“Managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2 server backed by S3 or EFS”
cards.a: AWS Transfer Family

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Transfer Family?
cards.a:
• Partners send files over SFTP and the data must land in S3
• Replace a self-managed SFTP server

cards.q: AWS Transfer Family: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Protocols: SFTP, FTPS, FTP (VPC only), AS2
• Storage in S3 or EFS
• Authentication: service-managed, AD, custom IdP (Lambda)
• Existing clients stay unchanged

cards.q: When is AWS Transfer Family NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Bulk data migration → DataSync/Snowball

cards.q: AWS Transfer Family vs AWS DataSync: what's the difference?
cards.a: DataSync — bulk migration; Transfer Family — file exchange protocol

cards.q: What is AWS Snow Family?
cards.a: Physical devices for offline data transfer and edge computing

cards.q:
Which Migration & Transfer service/concept is this?
“Physical devices for offline data transfer and edge computing”
cards.a: AWS Snow Family

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Snow Family?
cards.a:
• Tens to hundreds of TB over a slow/expensive link
• Data processing at remote locations without connectivity

cards.q: AWS Snow Family: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Snowball Edge Storage Optimized (~210 TB) and Compute Optimized (EC2/Lambda at the edge)
• Snowcone and Snowmobile have been discontinued
• Rule of thumb: if network transfer takes more than ~1 week, consider Snowball
• KMS encryption, data is imported into S3
• Works without network connectivity (edge)

cards.q:
AWS Snow Family — fill in the blank:

210 TB

Snowball Edge Storage Optimized (~210 TB) and Compute Optimized (EC2/Lambda at the edge)

cards.q:
AWS Snow Family — fill in the blank:
Rule of thumb: if network transfer takes more than ~_____, consider Snowball

1 week

cards.q: When is AWS Snow Family NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Recurring sync of small volumes → DataSync

cards.q: AWS Snow Family vs AWS DataSync: what's the difference?
cards.a: DataSync — online over the network; Snowball — offline device shipping

cards.q: AWS Snow Family vs AWS Direct Connect: what's the difference?
cards.a: DX — dedicated link, but takes weeks to provision

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Application Migration Service (MGN)?
cards.a:
• Move hundreds of servers to AWS as-is (rehost)

cards.q: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN): what are the key exam facts?

cards.q: When is AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Database-only migration → DMS

cards.q: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) vs AWS DMS: what's the difference?

cards.a: Single place to track migrations and discovery

cards.q:
Which Migration & Transfer service/concept is this?
“Single place to track migrations and discovery”
cards.a: AWS Migration Hub

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Migration Hub?
cards.a:
• Build an inventory and dependency map of on-prem servers before migration
• Track migration of many applications

cards.q: AWS Migration Hub: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Tracks migration progress across MGN, DMS, etc.

cards.q: When is AWS Migration Hub NOT the right choice?

cards.q: AWS Migration Hub vs AWS Application Migration Service (MGN): what's the difference?

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)?

• DR for on-prem servers into AWS with low RPO/RTO at low cost
• Pilot light–style DR for servers

cards.q: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS): what are the key exam facts?

• RPO in seconds, RTO in minutes
• Low-cost staging area; full resources launch on failover
• Sources: on-prem, other clouds, other AWS Regions
• Failback after recovery

cards.q: When is AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) NOT the right choice?
cards.a: • Not a scheduled backup tool (that's AWS Backup)

cards.q: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) vs AWS Backup: what's the difference?
cards.a: Backup — scheduled snapshots; DRS — continuous replication

cards.q: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) vs AWS Application Migration Service (MGN): what's the difference?
cards.a: MGN — migration; DRS — DR

cards.q: What is Amazon CloudWatch?
cards.a: Metrics, alarms, and dashboards for resources and applications

cards.q:
Which Management & Governance service/concept is this?
“Metrics, alarms, and dashboards for resources and applications”
cards.a: Amazon CloudWatch

cards.q: When would you choose Amazon CloudWatch?
cards.a:
• Alert when CPU > 80%
• Monitor EC2 memory → CloudWatch Agent
• Automatically recover an instance on host failure

cards.q: Amazon CloudWatch: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Standard EC2 metrics every 5 min, detailed monitoring — 1 min
• EC2 memory and disk are not collected by default → CloudWatch Agent
• Alarms → SNS, Auto Scaling, EC2 actions (recover, reboot, stop)
• Custom metrics, high-resolution down to 1 s; composite alarms
• Container Insights, Synthetics canaries, anomaly detection

cards.q: When is Amazon CloudWatch NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Who made an API call — that's CloudTrail
• Configuration history — that's Config

cards.q: Amazon CloudWatch vs AWS CloudTrail: what's the difference?
cards.a: CloudTrail — who called what (API audit); CloudWatch — metrics and performance

cards.q: Amazon CloudWatch vs AWS Config: what's the difference?
cards.a: Config — resource configurations and compliance

cards.q: Amazon CloudWatch vs AWS X-Ray: what's the difference?
cards.a: X-Ray — tracing requests across services

cards.q: What is CloudWatch Logs?
cards.a: Centralized log collection, storage, and analysis

cards.q:
Which Management & Governance service/concept is this?
“Centralized log collection, storage, and analysis”
cards.a: CloudWatch Logs

cards.q: When would you choose CloudWatch Logs?
cards.a:
• Collect application logs from EC2 (CloudWatch Agent)
• Alarm on errors in logs via a metric filter
• Stream logs to another system in real time

cards.q: CloudWatch Logs: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Log groups/streams, retention from 1 day to never expire
• Logs Insights — log query language
• Metric filters → metrics and alarms
• Subscription filters → Lambda, Firehose, OpenSearch (real-time)

Log groups/streams, retention from _____ to never expire

1 day

cards.a: OpenSearch — full-text search and advanced log analytics

cards.q: CloudWatch Logs vs AWS CloudTrail: what's the difference?
cards.a: CloudTrail can send events to CloudWatch Logs

cards.q: What is AWS CloudTrail?
cards.a: API call auditing: who did what, when, and from where in the account

cards.q:
Which Management & Governance service/concept is this?
“API call auditing: who did what, when, and from where in the account”
cards.a: AWS CloudTrail

cards.q: When would you choose AWS CloudTrail?
cards.a:
• Who deleted a resource / changed a security group
• Audit and investigate user actions
• React to a specific API call via EventBridge

cards.q: AWS CloudTrail: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• 90-day event history for free (management events)
• Trail → S3 (+ CloudWatch Logs) for long-term retention; organization trail
• Management events (on) vs data events (S3 object, Lambda invoke — paid, off by default)
• Log file integrity validation; CloudTrail Insights — unusual activity
• CloudTrail Lake — SQL queries over events

cards.q: When is AWS CloudTrail NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Performance metrics — CloudWatch
• Doesn't show current configuration state — Config
• Recording ≠ detecting: to be alerted on suspicious access patterns use GuardDuty (it analyzes CloudTrail)

cards.q: AWS CloudTrail vs Amazon CloudWatch: what's the difference?
cards.a: CloudWatch — metrics/logs; CloudTrail — API audit

cards.q: AWS CloudTrail vs AWS Config: what's the difference?
cards.a: Config — what changed in a resource's configuration; CloudTrail — who called the API

cards.q: AWS CloudTrail vs VPC Flow Logs: what's the difference?
cards.a: Flow Logs — network traffic, not API calls

cards.q: What is AWS Config?
cards.a: Resource configuration history and rule-based compliance evaluation

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Config?
cards.a:
• Verify all EBS volumes are encrypted / S3 buckets are not public
• See what a resource's configuration looked like in the past
• Automatically remediate non-compliance

cards.q: AWS Config: what are the key exam facts?
cards.a:
• Configuration items and a timeline of resource changes
• Config Rules (managed and custom via Lambda/Guard) — detective control
• Remediation via SSM Automation (automatic fix)
• Conformance packs; aggregator for multi-account/multi-region
• Regional; charged per configuration item and rule evaluation

cards.q: When is AWS Config NOT the right choice?
cards.a:
• Does not prevent actions (that's SCP/IAM)
• Doesn't show who called the API — CloudTrail
• Aggregator + conformance packs evaluate/deploy rules; they don't provision accounts (that's Control Tower)

cards.q: AWS Config vs AWS CloudTrail: what's the difference?
cards.a: CloudTrail — who called the API; Config — what the resulting state is

cards.q: AWS Config vs Service Control Policies (SCP): what's the difference?
cards.a: SCP — preventive; Config — detective

cards.q: AWS Config vs AWS Security Hub: what's the difference?
cards.a: Security Hub uses Config for standards checks

cards.q: What is AWS Systems Manager?

Which Management & Governance service/concept is this?

cards.a: AWS Systems Manager

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Systems Manager?
cards.a:
• Secure instance access without SSH/bastion
• Patch a fleet of EC2 and on-prem servers
• Store configuration/parameters cheaply

cards.q: AWS Systems Manager: what are the key exam facts?

• Run Command, Patch Manager, Maintenance Windows, State Manager

cards.q: When is AWS Systems Manager NOT the right choice?

cards.q: AWS Systems Manager vs AWS Secrets Manager: what's the difference?

cards.q: AWS Systems Manager vs AWS Config: what's the difference?
cards.a: Config detects; SSM Automation remediates

cards.q: When would you choose AWS Trusted Advisor?

• Quick account security check

cards.q: AWS Trusted Advisor: what are the key exam facts?

• Checks service quotas, open ports, public S3, MFA on root
